hints: Focus on the role of the solvent, as aqueous NaOH and ethanolic NaOH make hydroxide act in two very different ways.
Remember that water as solvent favours substitution of Br by OH to give ethanol, while ethanol as solvent favours removal of HBr to give an alkene.
Check if ethane-1,2-diol is even possible from bromoethane, which has only one bromine atom to replace.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two classic conditions**

Think of aqueous NaOH as a source of $OH^-$ for substitution, and ethanolic NaOH as a source of $OH^-$ for elimination. This is a key pattern to learn.

Aqueous: substitution to alcohol
Ethanolic: elimination to alkene

**Test statement 3 first**

Bromoethane with NaOH in water gives nucleophilic substitution.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Br}^-$$
So water to ethanol is correct. Statement 3 is true.

**Test statement 2 next**

Bromoethane with NaOH in ethanol gives elimination of HBr.
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Br}^-$$
So ethanol to ethene is correct. Statement 2 is true.

**Test statement 1 last**

Ethane-1,2-diol is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and needs two OH groups. Bromoethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$, has only one Br to substitute, so it can only form the mono-alcohol ethanol, not a diol. Statement 1 is false.

**Combine the verdict**

Only 2 and 3 are correct. That combination matches the correct option.

options.A: Incorrect because it includes statement 1. A diol needs two functional groups, but bromoethane has only one C-Br bond, so aqueous NaOH can only give ethanol, not ethane-1,2-diol.
options.B: Incorrect because it includes statement 1 and excludes statement 3. Statement 1 is impossible for a monobromoalkane, while statement 3 correctly describes aqueous substitution to ethanol.
options.C: Correct because only 2 and 3 are true. Aqueous NaOH (water) gives nucleophilic substitution to ethanol, and ethanolic NaOH (ethanol) gives elimination to ethene.
options.D: Incorrect because it includes only statement 3. While statement 3 is true, statement 2 is also true since hot ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation of bromoethane to ethene.
